newsitem.title: FRANCE: Giscard d'Estaing warns Paris on Maastricht target.
newsitem.headline: Giscard d'Estaing warns Paris on Maastricht target.

text.p: Former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing cautioned on Thursday that France would find it very difficult to meet European single currency criteria in late 1997 unless its economic growth quickened.

In a column for the weekly L'Express, Giscard d'Estaing wrote that he and former West German chancellor Helmut Schmidt had set two objectives for monetary union -- to give Europe a true international currency and to give member states a solid monetary basis for durable economic growth.

"This second result is essential: without stronger growth, France will have great difficulty in respecting honestly the Maastricht criteria in late 1997," wrote the centrist Giscard D'Estaing, who initiated the European Monetary System (EMS) with Schmidt in 1979.

"And I do not believe that our country should enter the great European monetary adventure in a weak economic and social condition," added the former president, a member of the UDF, junior partner in the ruling coalition.
The government has forecast economic growth to pick up to 2.3 percent next year from 1.3 percent this year.
The Maastricht treaty calls for would-be members of a single currency to meet a range of financial critieria in 1997 and schedules the final phase of monetary union for 1999.

Although monetary union has a serious chance of taking place, and the French financial system was actively preparing to adopt the euro currency, Giscard d'Estaing said one key question remained unanswered:

"Should France enter a durable monetary system with a languid economy, company heads demoralised and demotivated by excessive charges, the risk of international takeovers of its finest industrial assets and a sadly rigid unemployment rate?" he wrote.
He also criticised the Intergovernment Conference (IGC) on European Union (EU) institutional reform launched in Turin early this year which he said had so far yielded no result whatsoever.
He blamed a rush to announce an enlargement of the 15-member EU as soon as possible.
"Only a limited degree of integration can mark this greater Europe...on which we are from now on uncautiously, but irreversibly, committed," he wrote.
